body:
> I don't think it's a good idea to implement such a constructor. It's very dangerous and easy to miss the fact that a span is not a container and does not own the underlying buffer. 

I somewhat agree. `Span` _does_ have a very big disclaimer over its implementation that it does not own the underlying data. But it's probable that most people won't read this.

> This constructor saves a reference to a temporary object, so even if very experienced C++ developers can avoid that trap, it remains a trap which can be very hard to debug.

It's true that problems like this would be hard to debug.
On the bright side, it's a straight forward problem that will will likely be caught at the first test. It's not some obscure gotcha, it's a pretty in-the-face gotcha.

> Moreover, I think the current implementation has UB because there is no constraint on the constness of `T`. C++26 added this constructor in `std::span` with a `requires (std::is_const_v<T>)` to enforce the lifetime extension of the `std::initializer_list`.

Godot's `Span` _only_ stores `const` pointers. This is a conscious deviation from `std::span` which can also store mutable pointers. That's why there's no enforced lifetime extension here :)

> Also gcc produce warnings which must be disabled (-Winit-list-lifetime).

Interesting! That's not great.

On some more thought, it seems that directly allowing `std::initializer_list` is very hard to make safe to use. `Span` is simply not meant to _store_ values, but rather point to externally stored ones. The fact that it works when directly passing a `std::initializer_list` is more a side effect of how C++ handles temporaries, than an actual feature :wink: 

It's also rather unintuitive that this is safe:
```cpp
function_taking_span({1, 2, 3});
```
but the only way to factor the expression out introduces immediate UB:
```cpp
Span s = {1, 2, 3};
function_taking_span(s);
```
Extracting a variable isn't a change that people associate with undefined behavior, so it's likely to catch developers off-guard. It's also a workflow that is automated in many IDEs.

---

I like the suggestion with `std::array`, as that separates the data (storage) from the span (view). And it's still on the stack, so I'd expect the same assembly.

If typing `std::array { 1, 2, 3 }` is too long, there's potentially an alternative syntax:
```cpp
template <typename T, typename... Ts>
constexpr auto vals(T first, Ts... rest) {
    return std::array{first, rest...};
}
```
Usage:
```cpp
function_taking_span(vals(1, 2, 3));
```
And it can be safely refactored:
```cpp
std::array s = vals(1, 2, 3);
function_taking_span(s);
```
<sub>(One could still accidentally write `Span s = vals(...)`, but this actively changes the type of the expression, and won't be suggested by IDEs).</sub>

Returning is still a problem, but this is in the nature of spans, and I don't think one problem automatically justifies having more problems :slightly_smiling_face: anyway, just some brainstorming, I'm sure the API will end up nice either way :+1:

> On some more thought, it seems that directly allowing `std::initializer_list` is very hard to make safe to use. `Span` is simply not meant to _store_ values, but rather point to externally stored ones. The fact that it works when directly passing a `std::initializer_list` is more a side effect of how C++ handles temporaries, than an actual feature 😉

I think `Span` is just generally hard to make safe to use. The following will already compile but crash too, in the same vein as the examples you provided:

```c++
Span<char32_t> test = String("Test");
```

`String` will happily convert to Span and be deallocated immediately, leaving an invalid `Span` behind. Before `Span`, we had the same risk with pointer conversions:
```
char32_t *a = String("a");
```

In fact, the same 'arguments are OK, storage is not' conundrum is already quite prevalent in the codebase, in places like this:
https://github.com/godotengine/godot/blob/1f56d96cf2c768c3844c68ccb504dfeee841ae15/editor/export/project_zip_packer.cpp#L59

Here, `utf8()` is creating a temporary storage object, but `get_data()` is taking its pointer. If one tried to store the pointer in a variable (instead of the storage object), the code would be incorrect.

On the upside, the code will immediately crash on first use, so it's not exactly a hard bug to track down. I'm much more afraid of bugs that _sometimes_ crash than those that _always_ crash.
It's just something you have to be aware of when using `Span` in general. It could only truly be made safe with a rust-like borrow checker.

Regarding `std::array` and `vals`, I'd be _OK_ with `std::array` syntax, but it's pretty verbose, and likely wouldn't be a viable candidate to replace https://github.com/godotengine/godot/pull/103931 (which is currently implemented in `VectorView`).
I'm more opposed to `vals(1, 2, 3)` because of the changed syntax, but it would be possible to create a `struct vals` such that it could be used like `vals { 1, 2, 3 }`. This would be like `std::array`, just with a shorter struct name, I suppose.
